title: How (and Why) to Leave Audio Feedback on Student Work https://davestuartjr.com/how-and-why-to-leave-audio-feedback-on-student-work-distance-learning
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. surveys a 2007 study on asynchronous audio feedback, finding that students who received spoken comments on their work were significantly more satisfied and three times more likely to apply the feedback to future assignments than students who received text-only comments. He walks through the study's four explanatory themes — clearer conveyance of nuance and tone, a stronger sense of community and involvement, better retention of the feedback's content, and a greater perceived sense that the instructor cared — quoting student interview responses for each. Stuart is careful to flag the study's limitations (a small sample, unreplicated findings, and a 2015 study that found no attainment gains from audio feedback), concluding that the honest takeaway is increased satisfaction rather than guaranteed learning gains. He closes the piece by committing to try audio feedback himself and walking readers through how to record it inside several major learning management systems.
points: The 2007 study Stuart cites found students were three times more likely to apply audio feedback to subsequent work than text-only feedback.
Audio feedback's advantage is largely about tone and nuance — students in the study routinely misread the intent of written comments in ways that spoken feedback resolved instantly.
Students associated audio feedback with feeling cared for and connected, reducing the "dehumanizing" sense that can come with fully online coursework.
Stuart models good research literacy by naming the study's limitations (small, unreplicated, and contradicted by a 2015 follow-up) rather than overselling the intervention.
quotes: Students who received audio feedback were three times more likely to apply the contents of audio feedback to subsequent work.

When I write to a student something like, "not sure what you mean here" or "unclear," it can sound a dozen ways in the mind of the student. But when I speak that feedback, my tone is way harder to miss.
I've always felt that these online classes are a little, you know, dehumanizing. That said, I get this file where you put in this audio and boom! It was all a big change for me you know?
Because understanding that a strategy works is like being given the proverbial fish; understanding why a strategy works is learning to fish.
In fact, in a 2015 study I found, audio feedback did not lead to higher attainment on subsequent work.
As for me and my practice, I see enough potential gains to merit the challenges of trying to get the hang of leaving feedback this way. I'm going to try it, earnestly.
